meta.title: It is my film: Yojimbo and A Fistful of Dollars
meta.angle: a work and its remake, and the lawsuit between them

candide.instructions: Voice: the curious co-host of a two-voice podcast about movies. Affect: delighted, quick, a little teasing, genuinely surprised by what the expert says. Pacing: brisk and conversational, with real pauses before a question lands. Intonation: lively, rising on questions, falling on punchlines. Emphasis: stress the one word that carries the surprise. Never flat, never read aloud: you are talking to a friend across a table.

expert.instructions: Voice: the film expert of a two-voice podcast, the one who has seen everything and enjoys telling it. Affect: warm, amused, storytelling, with the pleasure of a good anecdote. Pacing: varied, speeds up on the narrative and slows down right before a reveal or a quotation; quotations are read a touch slower, as if from the page. Intonation: wide range, conversational, never a lecture, never a monotone. Emphasis: land the names and the numbers. You are telling this to a friend, not reading it.

beats.text: Picture this. A stranger walks into a town. Dust, silence, two gangs staring at each other across one street. He has no name, no past, and no intention of picking a side.
beats.delivery: Trailer voice, unhurried, intimate, as if leaning in.

beats.text: And he gets both gangs to wipe each other out.
beats.delivery: Finishing the sentence for him, knowing.

beats.text: Right. You have seen that movie. You have probably seen it twice, in two languages, without knowing it was the same movie.
Twice. Okay, which two?
beats.speech: <laugh> Twice. Okay, which two?

beats.text: Yojimbo, Akira Kurosawa, 1961. And A Fistful of Dollars, Sergio Leone, 1964. Three years apart, one story, and one lawsuit.
beats.delivery: Announcing the two titles like a boxing card.

beats.text: So that is the episode: same story, two films, and a lawsuit.
And here is the mission. We are not going to say these films are similar. We are going to show you how similar, scene by scene, and then where Leone actually changed things.
And the sources. Because I know you.

Three of them. The two films' entries in the database, which carry the full text of each film's page. The subtitles of the films themselves, so when we quote a line, it is the line. And the database's own graph: who adapted what from whom.
beats.delivery: Counting on fingers, precise, proud of it.

beats.text: No numbers from memory.
No numbers from memory. If I cannot source it, I do not say it.
beats.speech: No numbers from memory. If I cannot source it, |mm-hm| I do not say it.

beats.text: Okay. Let's get it out of the way. Leone copied Kurosawa. End of story?
beats.delivery: Mock-impatient, as if settling a bet.

beats.text: Let me read you a letter instead. It is short. Signor Leone, I have just had the chance to see your film. It is a very fine film, but it is my film.
beats.speech: Let me read you a letter instead. It is short. <short pause> Signor Leone, I have just had the chance to see your film. It is a very fine film... <short pause> but it is MY film.

source.quote: Signor Leone, I have just had the chance to see your film. It is a very fine film, but it is my film. Since Japan is a signatory of the Berne Convention on the international copyright, you must pay me.

brick.text: It is a very fine film, but it is my film.

beats.delivery: Reads the letter as a letter: slow, courteous, a faint smile on 'my film'.

beats.text: It is my film. That is the most polite threat I have ever heard.
beats.speech: <gasp> It is my film. That is the most polite threat I have ever heard.

beats.text: Wait for the next sentence. Since Japan is a signatory of the Berne Convention on the international copyright, you must pay me.
beats.speech: <chuckle> Wait for the next sentence. Since Japan is a signatory of the Berne Convention on the international copyright... you must pay me.

source.quote: Signor Leone, I have just had the chance to see your film. It is a very fine film, but it is my film. Since Japan is a signatory of the Berne Convention on the international copyright, you must pay me.

beats.text: So, a lawyer's letter with a bow on it. Did he pay?
Not at first. Toho sued. Leone ignored the lawsuit.

source.quote: Leone ignored the resulting lawsuit, but eventually settled out of court, reportedly for 15% of the worldwide receipts of A Fistful of Dollars and over $100,000.

brick.caption: Fifteen percent of the worldwide receipts

beats.text: Of course he did.
Then he settled out of court. Fifteen percent of the worldwide receipts, plus over one hundred thousand dollars.
beats.speech: Then he settled out of court. Fifteen percent of the worldwide receipts. |wow| Plus over one hundred thousand dollars.

source.quote: Leone ignored the resulting lawsuit, but eventually settled out of court, reportedly for 15% of the worldwide receipts of A Fistful of Dollars and over $100,000.

beats.delivery: Landing the numbers one by one.

beats.text: Wait, wait. Fifteen percent of the whole film?
Of the worldwide receipts. And here is the line I love from the entry: Kurosawa earned more money from this settlement than from Yojimbo.

source.quote: Kurosawa earned more money from this settlement than from Yojimbo.

beats.delivery: Slowing down for the reveal, delighted.

beats.text: More from being copied than from the original.
beats.speech: <laugh> More from being copied than from the original.

beats.text: More from being copied than from the original. Hold that thought. We come back to it at the end.
How big was the film, though? Fifteen percent of what?
The budget was two hundred thousand dollars.
That is nothing. Even then.
And it sold nearly fifteen million tickets in Italy alone, and grossed more than nineteen point nine million dollars worldwide.

source.quote: It sold admissions of 14,797,275 ticket sales in Italy.
totaling more than $19.9 million grossed worldwide

beats.text: So, roughly a hundred times the budget. How did it even get released?
beats.delivery: Doing the sum out loud, then curious.

beats.text: Badly. No major distributor wanted a faux-Western by an unknown director. It came out in Italy on the twelfth of September 1964, typically the worst month for sales, and the Italian critics shunned it.

source.quote: The film ended up being released in Italy 12 September 1964, which was typically the worst month for sales.
The film was initially shunned by Italian critics, who gave it extremely negative reviews.

beats.delivery: Storytelling, a shrug in the voice.

beats.text: And then?
It spread at a grassroots level. By the end of its run: 2.7 billion lire, more than any other Italian film to that point.

source.quote: it grossed 2.7 billion lire ($4,375,000) in Italy, more than any other Italian film to that point.

beats.text: And it hid its accent.
Its accent?
Few spaghetti Westerns had reached the United States, so the Europeans took American-sounding names. Leone became Bob Robertson.

source.quote: These included Leone ("Bob Robertson"), Gian Maria Volonté ("Johnny Wels") and the composer, Ennio Morricone ("Dan Savio").

beats.text: Bob Robertson.
beats.speech: <laugh> Bob Robertson.

beats.text: Gian Maria Volonté, the villain, became Johnny Wels. And the composer, Ennio Morricone: Dan Savio.

source.quote: These included Leone ("Bob Robertson"), Gian Maria Volonté ("Johnny Wels") and the composer, Ennio Morricone ("Dan Savio").

beats.text: Dan Savio. So it is an Italian film pretending to be American...
beats.delivery: Setting up the punchline, trailing off.

beats.text: ...shot in Spain, mostly near Hoyo de Manzanares, close to Madrid, and in the Tabernas Desert of Almería.

source.quote: A Fistful of Dollars was shot in Spain, mostly near Hoyo de Manzanares close to Madrid

beats.delivery: Picking up her sentence without a gap.

beats.text: Pretending to be Mexico.
Pretending to be Mexico. We will get to how they even talked to each other on that set.
Okay. To see what Leone took, you have to start with the blueprint. Yojimbo. The title means bodyguard, by the way.

source.quote: lit. Bodyguard

beats.delivery: Shifting gears, calm, the teacher's voice for one line.

beats.text: Fine. But was it really a copy, or just the same kind of story?
Let me put them side by side, and you tell me. Same opening. An innkeeper explains the war to the stranger.

source.quote: The owner Gonji advises the rōnin to leave, and tells him that the two warring bosses, Ushitora and Seibei, are fighting over the lucrative gambling trade run by Seibei.
Silvanito, the town's innkeeper, tells the Stranger about a feud between two smuggler families vying to gain control of the town

brick.caption: “The Baxters on one side. The Rojos on the other.” (00:31:56)

beats.text: The innkeeper is the exposition guy.
In Yojimbo it is Gonji, and the two bosses are Ushitora and Seibei. In San Miguel it is Silvanito: the Baxters on one side, the Rojos on the other.

source.quote: The owner Gonji advises the rōnin to leave, and tells him that the two warring bosses, Ushitora and Seibei, are fighting over the lucrative gambling trade run by Seibei.
Silvanito, the town's innkeeper, tells the Stranger about a feud between two smuggler families vying to gain control of the town

source.line: The Baxters on one side. The Rojos on the other.

beats.delivery: Clear, parallel structure, hands moving left and right.

beats.text: Same demonstration of force. The samurai kills three of Ushitora's men to get hired.
And the gunman?
Shoots the four men who insulted him on his way in.

source.quote: He demonstrates his deadliness to both sides by shooting to death with ease the four men who insulted him as he entered town.

beats.text: Four. He is already outbidding.
And the coffin maker counts. On his way to the fight, Sanjuro orders two coffins. Then he corrects himself: no, better make that three.

source.line: Casket maker. Two coffins.
No, better make that three.

beats.delivery: Relishing the joke, a beat before 'three'.

beats.text: He revises the estimate.
beats.speech: <laugh> He revises the estimate.

beats.text: In San Miguel the stranger says: get three coffins ready. He comes back: my mistake. Four coffins.
beats.speech: In San Miguel the stranger says: get three coffins ready. He comes back: <short pause> my mistake. Four coffins.

source.line: Get three coffins ready.
My mistake. Four coffins.

beats.text: Same joke, one more body.
One more body. Leone keeps the joke and raises the count. That is the whole film in one line.
And the names? The samurai has one, doesn't he?
He makes one up. He is asked his name, he looks at a mulberry field: Kuwabatake Sanjuro. Mulberry field, thirty years old.

source.quote: When asked his name, the samurai calls himself "Kuwabatake Sanjuro", which he seems to make up while looking at a mulberry field by the town.

source.line: Sanjuro Kuwabatake... (30-year-old Mulberry Field)

beats.delivery: Amused, as if watching him do it.

beats.text: He names himself after the scenery.
The entry calls him an early man with no name. Leone's stranger gets even less: the entry only ever calls him the Stranger, and one line of the film calls him Joe.

source.quote: When asked his name, the samurai calls himself "Kuwabatake Sanjuro", which he seems to make up while looking at a mulberry field by the town.
An unnamed stranger arrives at the little frontier town of San Miguel.

source.line: Joe, I have prepared the wagon

beats.text: Joe. Once.

Once. Then the beats line up, one after the other. A lie planted in both camps. A woman handed over for a debt. The hero found out, beaten, escaping in a coffin. And coming back because the innkeeper has been taken.

source.line: Twenty-five in advance, with room and board.
The rest when you're all done.

left.caption: “Twenty-five in advance, with room and board.” (00:21:03)

beats.text: Take them one at a time. The woman.
In Yojimbo she is Nui, a farmer's wife. Her husband sold her to Ushitora to settle a gambling debt, and Ushitora gave her to the brewer Tokuemon as chattel, to gain his support.

source.quote: Sanjuro learns that the mistress, Nui, is a local farmer's wife. After he sold her to Ushitora to settle a gambling debt, Ushitora gave her to Tokuemon as chattel to gain his support.

source.line: Nui!

beats.delivery: Storytelling, a touch of disgust on 'chattel'.

beats.text: As chattel. Nice people.
In Fistful she is Marisol. Ramón accused her husband Julio of cheating at cards and took her as collateral.

source.quote: He learns from Silvanito that Ramón accused Julio of cheating during a card game and took Marisol as collateral.

source.line: Marisol!

beats.text: Collateral. Same transaction, different currency.
Then the same good deed, with the same hardness. He kills the guards, frees her, gives the family money and orders them to leave town at once.

source.quote: Sanjuro kills the guards and reunites the woman with her husband and son. He gives them some money and orders them to leave town immediately.

source.line: Here's 30 ryo. I stole it from Ushitora.

left.caption: “Here's 30 ryo. I stole it from Ushitora.” (01:08:53)

beats.text: Orders them.
Orders them. And Leone adds one touch: the stranger wrecks the house, to make it look like a Baxter attack.

source.quote: the Stranger kills the guards, frees Marisol, and wrecks the house where she was held to create the appearance of an attack by the Baxters. He gives money to Marisol and urges her family to leave town.

source.line: Go. Go to him, Marisol.

beats.text: A cover story. That is new?
That is new.
And he gets caught, right?

source.line: This is the gate to hell.
You are behaving like a stubborn idiot.

right.caption: “You are behaving like a stubborn idiot.” (01:09:34)

beats.text: Both times. In Yojimbo, Unosuke grows suspicious of Nui's escape and uncovers the betrayal. Sanjuro is beaten, imprisoned and tortured.

source.line: I know I'm quite a sight, but could you do your staring later?

source.quote: Unosuke becomes suspicious of Sanjuro and the circumstances surrounding Nui's escape, eventually uncovering evidence

left.caption: “I know I'm quite a sight, but could you do your staring later?” (01:30:01)

beats.text: Then he is smuggled out of town in a coffin by Gonji, and recovers in a small temple near a cemetery.

source.quote: Smuggled out of town in a coffin by Gonji
He then recuperates in a small temple near a cemetery.

beats.text: In a coffin. The coffin maker's finest hour.
And in San Miguel: the Rojos discover who freed Marisol, capture and torture the stranger. Piripero, the coffin maker, gets him out in a coffin, and he recovers in an abandoned mine.

source.quote: With help from the local coffinmaker named Piripero, the Stranger escapes town by hiding in a coffin, and recuperates in an abandoned mine.

source.line: But you're not dead yet.

beats.text: Temple, mine. Same exit, different real estate.
And the return has the same trigger: the innkeeper. Gonji is captured by Ushitora. Silvanito is captured and tortured by the Rojos for the stranger's whereabouts.

source.quote: Upon learning that Gonji has been captured by Ushitora, Sanjuro returns to town
When Piripero tells him that Silvanito has been captured and tortured by the Rojos for the Stranger's whereabouts, he returns to town to confront them.

beats.text: It's me! Gonji's in trouble! There is literally a line for it.

source.line: It's me! Gonji's in trouble!

beats.delivery: Quoting the subtitle, half-shouting it, then laughing.

beats.text: Okay. I need to play devil's advocate here. Everything you have listed is a plot. Stranger, two gangs, a woman, a beating, a coffin. Isn't that just the genre?
Fair. So let's look at what Leone dropped, and what he added. That is where you see the hand.
Because so far it is the same film with hats.
Not quite. Leone drops three things: the official whose arrival stops the first battle, the mayor going mad, and the farmer's son who closes the story.

right.caption: “Murderers! I hope you rot in hell!” (01:24:06)

brick.caption: What Leone drops, what he adds

beats.text: And adds?
The massacre of a gold escort, the Baxter house burning with everyone inside, and the steel plate under the poncho.

source.line: Murderers! I hope you rot in hell!

beats.text: What official? Tell me about the one Leone dropped.

A bugyō. A government official from Edo. Sanjuro has just set the two gangs against each other, he expects a massacre... and the official arrives. Both sides retreat without a drop of blood. The plan is foiled.
beats.speech: A bugyō. A government official from Edo. Sanjuro has just set the two gangs against each other, he expects a massacre... <short pause> and the official arrives. Both sides retreat without a drop of blood. The plan is foiled.

source.quote: His plan is foiled due to the unexpected arrival of a bugyō (a government official), which prompts both Seibei and Ushitora to make a bloodless retreat.

source.line: An inspector from Edo is coming!

brick.caption: Sanjuro on the watchtower, waiting for the massacre

beats.delivery: Storytelling, the anticlimax played for comedy.

beats.text: The one thing a samurai cannot fight: an inspector.
beats.speech: <laugh> The one thing a samurai cannot fight: an inspector.

beats.text: He leaves to investigate the assassination of a fellow official in another town. And the assassins, talking in Gonji's tavern, hand Sanjuro his next lever: he captures them and sells them to Seibei.

source.quote: The bugyō leaves soon after to investigate the assassination of a fellow official in another town. Overhearing the assassins discussing the hit in Gonji's tavern, Sanjuro later captures them and sells them to Seibei.

beats.text: So the plot runs on eavesdropping.

On eavesdropping. Leone replaces that whole mechanism with gold. The Rojos massacre a detachment of Mexican soldiers escorting a chest of gold, to exchange for rifles. The stranger props two of the dead up at the cemetery and sells both families the story of two survivors.

source.quote: The Stranger witnesses the Rojos massacre a detachment of Mexican soldiers escorting a chest of gold (to exchange for rifles) and comes up with a plan. He takes two of the dead bodies to a nearby cemetery and props them up to make them appear alive.

brick.caption: “Too still to be wounded. More like dummies.” (00:42:28)

beats.text: Two of those soldiers got away. They are hiding out in the cemetery.

source.line: Two of those soldiers got away. They are hiding out in the cemetery.

beats.delivery: Reading the subtitle in a bad conspirator's whisper.

beats.text: And someone finally looks closer: too still to be wounded. More like dummies.

source.line: Too still to be wounded. More like dummies.

beats.text: More like dummies.
beats.speech: <laugh> More like dummies.

beats.text: And the endings? Same exit, you said.

Same exit, different last gestures. Sanjuro spares a terrified young man, the farmer's son from the opening, and sends him home. The deranged mayor Tazaemon comes out in a samurai outfit, stabs the brewer to death, and Sanjuro orders him to kill himself.

source.quote: He spares a terrified young man, the son of the elderly couple from the opening, and sends him back to his parents. As Sanjuro surveys the damage, a now deranged Tazaemon comes out of his home in a samurai outfit and stabs Tokuemon to death.

beats.text: That is bleak.
Leone ends on a gunshot instead: Esteban aims at the stranger's back from a building, and Silvanito shoots him dead.

source.quote: Esteban aims for the Stranger's back from a nearby building, but is shot dead by Silvanito.

beats.text: The steel plate! That is the scene everyone remembers.

source.line: When a man with a .45 meets a man with a rifle,
you said the man with the pistol's a dead man.

brick.caption: “When a man with a .45 meets a man with a rifle, you said the man with the pistol's a dead man.” (01:34:49)

beats.text: And it is Leone's. In Yojimbo the duel is a pistol against a sword.

brick.caption: “When you want to kill a man, you must shoot for his heart.” (00:58:26)

beats.text: A sword against a gun. He should lose.
Leone keeps the idea, Ramón's Winchester against a man who seems unarmed, and adds the armor. And Ramón had said it himself, much earlier: when you want to kill a man, you must shoot for his heart.

source.line: When you want to kill a man, you must shoot for his heart.

beats.delivery: Setting the trap, quoting Ramón with a sneer.

beats.text: When a man with a .45 meets a man with a rifle, you said the man with the pistol's a dead man.

source.line: When a man with a .45 meets a man with a rifle,
you said the man with the pistol's a dead man.

beats.delivery: Reading Joe's line, slow, enjoying it.

beats.text: He quotes Ramón back to him. The plot is Kurosawa's. The punchline is Leone's.
Okay. Leave the plot. What does Leone do that Kurosawa doesn't?

Faces. The entry calls it the first film to show Leone's style, influenced by John Ford's landscapes and by Kurosawa's method, and he wanted an operatic feel. Extreme close-ups, functioning like arias in a traditional opera.

source.quote: This was influenced by both John Ford's cinematic landscaping and the Japanese method of direction honed by Akira Kurosawa.
so there are many examples of extreme closeups of the faces of different characters, functioning like arias in a traditional opera

beats.text: Arias. Just eyes and music.
Lit with Renaissance-type lighting effects. Portraits, basically.

source.quote: often lit with Renaissance-type lighting effects

beats.text: And the look. The poncho, the cigar. Who designed that?
Eastwood. Himself. Black jeans from a sports shop on Hollywood Boulevard. The hat from a Santa Monica wardrobe firm. The cigars from a Beverly Hills store.

source.quote: He bought black jeans from a sports shop on Hollywood Boulevard; the hat came from a Santa Monica wardrobe firm; and the trademark cigars from a Beverly Hills store.

brick.text: More than an actor, I needed a mask.

beats.text: He went shopping.
And he brought props from Rawhide: the Colt, the gunbelt, the spurs. The poncho was found in Spain.
beats.speech: <chuckle> And he brought props from Rawhide: the Colt, the gunbelt, the spurs. The poncho was found in Spain.

source.quote: He also brought props from Rawhide, including a Cobra-handled Colt, a gunbelt and spurs. The poncho was acquired in Spain.

beats.text: And the cigar? Does he even smoke?
He does not. The entry says the foul taste of the cigar put him in the right frame of mind for the character.

source.quote: although Eastwood is a non-smoker, he felt that the foul taste of the cigar in his mouth put him in the right frame of mind for his character

beats.text: Method acting by cigar.
And then Leone, on his star. More than an actor, I needed a mask. And Eastwood, at that time, only had two expressions: with hat and no hat.
beats.speech: And then Leone, on his star. More than an actor, I needed a mask. And Eastwood, at that time, only had two expressions: <short pause> with hat, and no hat.

source.quote: More than an actor, I needed a mask, and Eastwood, at that time, only had two expressions: with hat and no hat.

beats.delivery: Quoting Leone with relish, pause before the punchline.

beats.text: With hat and no hat. Harsh.
beats.speech: <laugh> With hat and no hat. Harsh.

beats.text: Harsh. And exactly what the film needed.
And the music? Everyone whistles that theme.
Ennio Morricone. Credited as Dan Savio, remember.

source.quote: The film's music was written by Ennio Morricone, initially credited as Dan Savio.

brick.text: He often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end.

beats.text: Dan Savio!

Leone asked for a theme close to Dimitri Tiomkin's El Degüello, from Rio Bravo. Morricone says he took a lullaby he had written before and developed it, and that the resemblance is in the execution, not the arrangement.

source.quote: Leone requested Morricone to write a theme that would be similar to Dimitri Tiomkin's El Degüello (used in Rio Bravo).

beats.text: A lullaby.
And some of the music was written before the film, which Morricone calls unusual. Leone often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end.

source.quote: he often kept the scenes longer simply because he didn't want the music to end.

beats.delivery: Slowing down on the last sentence.

beats.text: So those long stares... that is him not wanting to cut the music.
That is what Morricone says. And there is a quarrel here too.

source.quote: Leone said, "That's it", with Tevis claiming that the tune and musical arrangements were copied for the music for the opening title, "Titoli".

beats.text: Another one?

In 1962 the folk singer Peter Tevis had recorded Woody Guthrie's Pastures of Plenty, in a Morricone arrangement. When the record was played at a meeting about the film, Leone said: that's it. Tevis claims the tune and the arrangements were copied for the opening title, Titoli.

source.quote: Leone said, "That's it", with Tevis claiming that the tune and musical arrangements were copied for the music for the opening title, "Titoli".

beats.text: So the film about a copy opens on a disputed copy.
You could say that.
beats.speech: <chuckle> You could say that.

beats.text: And Kurosawa's side? Is there a theme?
Masaru Sato, who said his main influence was Henry Mancini.

source.quote: a loud, witty soundtrack by Masaru Sato, who said his main influence was Henry Mancini.

brick.text: The sound of his mind, discordant and undefeated and unserious.

beats.text: Mancini? In a samurai film?

Michael Wood, in the London Review of Books, hears drums, Japanese flutes mixed with American big band noises: jaunty and jangling throughout, discreetly off, as if half the band was playing in the wrong key.

source.quote: feels jaunty and jangling throughout, discreetly off, as if half the band was playing in the wrong key

beats.text: In the wrong key.
beats.speech: <laugh> In the wrong key.

beats.text: And he calls it the sound of Sanjuro's mind: discordant and undefeated and unserious.

source.quote: the sound of his mind, discordant and undefeated and unserious

beats.text: Discordant and undefeated. I want that on a T-shirt.
Okay, now the part I don't get. Kurosawa says: it is my film. So where did Kurosawa get it?
From Dashiell Hammett, by his own account. He named The Glass Key, the 1942 film noir made from Hammett's 1931 novel.

source.quote: Kurosawa stated that a major source for the plot was the 1942 film noir classic The Glass Key, an adaptation of Dashiell Hammett's 1931 novel of the same name.
